focus: visual comparison layer for Central Texas Poaceae

comparison_cards.title: Three awns vs one awn
comparison_cards.look_first: Pick one mature fertile floret and count the awns.

right.diagnostic: One conspicuous long twisted/bent awn on the fertile floret.

comparison_cards.tie_breaker: Three awns = Aristida; one long twisted awn = Nassella leucotricha.

comparison_cards.title: Switchgrass vs Indiangrass before flowering
comparison_cards.look_first: Pull a leaf blade away from the culm and inspect the collar region.

left.diagnostic: Dense cluster/ring of long white hairs at the blade base/collar, with a membranous ligule.
supporting: large open airy panicle when flowering

right.diagnostic: Paired upright 'rabbit-ear' / 'gun-sight' horns at the collar; nodes may be hairy.
supporting: more contracted silky awned panicle when flowering

comparison_cards.tie_breaker: White hairy 'armpit' = switchgrass; upright collar horns = Indiangrass.

comparison_cards.title: Grass vs sedge vs rush
comparison_cards.look_first: Run your fingers down the stem and look for nodes before worrying about the flower head.

Cyperaceae: usually solid and often triangular culm
Juncaceae: small flowers with 6 tepals and a capsule

comparison_cards.tie_breaker: Nodes strongly favor grass; triangular solid culm strongly favors sedge; round solid node-less culm plus 6-tepaled flowers favors rush.
comparison_cards.caution: These are field heuristics with exceptions; reproductive structures confirm the family.

comparison_cards.title: Two-door grass ID workflow
comparison_cards.look_first: Choose the door based on whether the plant is flowering.
comparison_cards.teaching_rule: Do not identify a grass from panicle color or overall fuzziness alone.
